John Keats. The English Romantic poet whose lyrical genius earned him rapid fame that has only grown since his death from tuberculosis at age twenty-five. Though his career lasted merely five years, his odes and narrative poems rank among the finest in English literature, celebrated for their sensory richness and philosophical depth.

Born in London to a middle-class family, he trained as an apothecary but abandoned medicine to pursue poetry full-time—a romantic but precarious choice. Between 1817 and 1820, he published three volumes of poetry, gaining recognition quickly within literary circles despite harsh reviews from major periodicals.

His most celebrated works came in 1819: the Ode to a Nightingale, Ode on a Grecian Urn, To Autumn, and La Belle Dame sans Merci, all works of extraordinary emotional and sensory power. He coined the phrase "negative capability," the capacity to exist in doubt and uncertainty without reaching for easy answers, which became a cornerstone of his poetic philosophy.

He contracted tuberculosis and moved to Rome seeking a warmer climate, but died there in 1821 at twenty-five, largely unknown outside literary circles. His sonnet On First Looking Into Chapman's Homer celebrates the emotional impact of discovering an old translation, demonstrating his capacity for sublime aesthetic response.

His love for Fanny Brawne, whom he met in 1818, became a consuming passion. Their relationship and his illness are intertwined in his late poetry and letters. Modern literary criticism views Keats as having achieved in five years what many poets never accomplish—a complete poetic vision combining sensory precision with philosophical depth. His letters, considered among the finest in English literature, reveal his aesthetic thinking and his struggle between love, ambition, and disease.
